content.value: Docker lets you run containers on a single computer. But what happens when you have 500 containers running across 50 servers in the cloud? That's where **Kubernetes** (also called K8s) comes in.

Kubernetes is like the **Captain of a ship** filled with containers. If a container crashes, Kubernetes restarts it. If traffic spikes, Kubernetes scales up extra containers. If a server dies, Kubernetes moves the containers to a healthy server.

K8s abbreviation: 'K' followed by 8 letters ('ubernete'), ending in 's' = K-eight-s. Google created it internally (called 'Borg'), then open-sourced it in 2014.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of Kubernetes?
options: To edit code in the browser
To automate deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications
To install operating systems on laptops
quiz.explanation: Kubernetes is an orchestration platform designed to automate container management across multiple servers.

content.value: A **Pod** is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It wraps one or more containers that share the same network namespace (same IP address and ports) and storage volumes. Think of a Pod as a tiny apartment — the containers inside share the same address and mailbox.

        C1["📦 App Container\nnginx:alpine"]
        C2["📊 Sidecar Container\nlog-collector"]
        VOL[("📁 Shared Volume")]
    end
    C1 --> VOL
    C2 --> VOL
    NET["🌐 Pod IP: 10.1.0.5"] --> POD

content.title: Pod Manifest (pod.yaml)
content.value:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-app
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:alpine
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80
      resources:
        requests:
          memory: "64Mi"
          cpu: "250m"
        limits:
          memory: "128Mi"
          cpu: "500m"

content.title: Pod Commands
content.value:
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml       # Create a pod from YAML
kubectl get pods                # List all pods
kubectl describe pod my-app     # Detailed info and events
kubectl logs my-app             # View container logs
kubectl exec -it my-app -- sh   # Shell into the pod
kubectl delete pod my-app       # Delete the pod
In practice, you rarely create Pods directly. Instead, you create Deployments that manage Pods for you. Deployments add self-healing, scaling, and rolling updates.

quiz.question: What do containers inside the same Pod share?
options: The same network namespace (IP address) and storage volumes
quiz.explanation: Containers in the same Pod share the same network namespace (same IP, can use localhost) and can mount shared volumes. This is useful for sidecar patterns like log collectors.

content.value: A **Deployment** is the most common way to run applications in Kubernetes. It manages a set of identical Pods (called replicas) and provides self-healing: if a Pod crashes, the Deployment automatically creates a replacement. If you need more capacity, just increase the replica count.

content.title: Deployment Self-Healing
content.value:
sequenceDiagram participant D as Deployment
replicas: 3 participant RS as ReplicaSet participant P1 as Pod 1 ✅ participant P2 as Pod 2 ✅ participant P3 as Pod 3 💀 D->>RS: Ensure 3 replicas running RS->>P1: Running RS->>P2: Running RS->>P3: Crashed! RS->>RS: Detected: only 2/3 running RS->>P3: Auto-create replacement Pod Note over RS,P3: Self-healing complete
3/3 Pods healthy

content.title: Deployment Manifest
content.value:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 3                    # Run 3 identical pods
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:                      # Pod template
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.25
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "100m"
              memory: "64Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "200m"
              memory: "128Mi"

content.title: Deployment Commands
content.value:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml         # Create/update deployment
kubectl get deployments                  # List deployments
kubectl scale deployment web-app --replicas=5  # Scale to 5 pods
kubectl rollout status deployment web-app  # Watch rollout progress
kubectl rollout undo deployment web-app    # Rollback to previous version

Interview question: 'How does Kubernetes achieve self-healing?' Answer: The Deployment controller continuously compares the desired state (3 replicas) with the actual state. If a Pod dies, the controller creates a new one to match the desired state. This is called the 'reconciliation loop'.

quiz.question: What happens if a Pod managed by a Deployment crashes?
options: The Deployment automatically creates a new Pod to replace it
You must manually restart the server
quiz.explanation: Deployments maintain a desired replica count. If a Pod dies, K8s self-heals by launching a new Pod automatically.

content.value: Pods are ephemeral — they can be created, destroyed, and replaced at any time. Their IP addresses change with every restart. A **Service** gives your Pods a stable network address and acts as an internal load balancer, distributing traffic across all healthy Pods.

    end

content.title: Service Manifest
content.value:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP              # Internal only (default)
  selector:
    app: web                   # Route to Pods with label app=web
  ports:
    - port: 80                 # Service port
      targetPort: 80           # Container port
      protocol: TCP

**ClusterIP** (default) — Internal only. Other pods reach it by name: `http://web-service:80`

**NodePort** — Exposes on every node's IP at a high port (30000-32767). Good for development.

**LoadBalancer** — Creates a cloud load balancer with a public IP. Used in AWS/GCP/Azure production.

Interview tip: 'How do pods discover each other?' Answer: Through DNS. K8s runs an internal DNS server (CoreDNS). If you create a Service called 'database', any pod can reach it at 'http://database' or 'database.namespace.svc.cluster.local'.

quiz.question: Why do we need Services in Kubernetes?
options: Because Pods can't communicate at all
To give Pods a stable network address since Pod IPs change on restart
quiz.explanation: Pods are ephemeral and get new IPs when replaced. Services provide a stable DNS name and IP, plus load balance traffic across all matching Pods.

content.value: Configuration should never be hardcoded inside your Docker image. **ConfigMaps** store non-sensitive configuration (database URLs, feature flags), and **Secrets** store sensitive data (passwords, API keys, TLS certificates). Both are injected into Pods at runtime.

content.title: ConfigMap & Secret Injection
content.value:
graph LR
    CM["📋 ConfigMap\nDATABASE_HOST=db\nLOG_LEVEL=info"] -->|env vars or volume| POD["📦 Pod"]
    SEC["🔐 Secret\nDB_PASSWORD=abc123\nAPI_KEY=xyz789"] -->|env vars or volume| POD
    style CM fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style SEC fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style POD fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: ConfigMap and Secret YAML
content.value:
# ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  DATABASE_HOST: "postgres-service"
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  MAX_CONNECTIONS: "100"
---
# Secret (values are base64 encoded)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: app-secrets
type: Opaque
data:
  DB_PASSWORD: cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=   # echo -n 'password123' | base64
  API_KEY: bXlzZWNyZXRrZXk=       # echo -n 'mysecretkey' | base64

content.title: Using ConfigMap and Secret in a Pod
content.value:
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:v1
      envFrom:                    # Load ALL keys as env vars
        - configMapRef:
            name: app-config
        - secretRef:
            name: app-secrets
      # Or mount as files:
      volumeMounts:
        - name: config-volume
          mountPath: /etc/config
  volumes:
    - name: config-volume
      configMap:
        name: app-config

Secrets are base64-encoded, NOT encrypted. Anyone with access to the cluster can decode them. For production, use a Secrets Manager like HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or enable Kubernetes Secrets encryption at rest.

quiz.question: What is the difference between ConfigMaps and Secrets?
options: ConfigMaps store non-sensitive config; Secrets store sensitive data like passwords
ConfigMaps are for production; Secrets are for development
ConfigMaps are YAML; Secrets are JSON
quiz.explanation: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive configuration (feature flags, URLs). Secrets hold sensitive data (passwords, API keys) and are base64-encoded with restricted access.

content.value: An **Ingress** is a K8s resource that manages external HTTP/HTTPS access to your services. Think of it as a smart reverse proxy — it routes traffic based on hostnames and URL paths to different backend services.

content.title: Ingress Routing Example
content.value:
graph LR
    USER["🌐 User Request"] --> ING["Ingress Controller\n(nginx / traefik)"]
    ING -->|"api.myapp.com/users"| SVC1["Users Service"]
    ING -->|"api.myapp.com/orders"| SVC2["Orders Service"]
    ING -->|"myapp.com/*"| SVC3["Frontend Service"]
    SVC1 --> P1["Pod"] & P2["Pod"]
    SVC2 --> P3["Pod"]
    SVC3 --> P4["Pod"] & P5["Pod"]
    style ING fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style SVC1 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style SVC2 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style SVC3 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#8b5cf6,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: Ingress Manifest with TLS
content.value:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: app-ingress
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - myapp.com
      secretName: tls-secret
  rules:
    - host: myapp.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api-service
                port:
                  number: 80
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: frontend-service
                port:
                  number: 80
An Ingress resource alone does nothing — you need an Ingress Controller (like nginx-ingress or traefik) running in your cluster to actually implement the routing rules.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a Kubernetes Ingress?
options: To route external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to internal services based on hostnames and paths
quiz.explanation: Ingress manages external HTTP/HTTPS access to services, providing host-based and path-based routing, TLS termination, and load balancing.

content.value: **Namespaces** divide a single cluster into virtual mini-clusters. Think of them as separate floors in an office building — each team gets their own floor with isolated resources. Common namespaces: `default`, `kube-system`, `production`, `staging`.

content.title: Namespace Commands
content.value:
kubectl get namespaces                   # List all namespaces
kubectl create namespace staging         # Create a namespace
kubectl get pods -n staging              # List pods in a specific namespace
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces        # List pods across ALL namespaces
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=staging  # Set default namespace

**Helm** is the package manager for Kubernetes — like apt for Ubuntu or npm for Node.js. A **Helm Chart** is a package of pre-configured Kubernetes YAML manifests. Instead of writing 10+ YAML files manually, you install a chart with one command.

content.title: Helm Commands
content.value:
# Install a chart from a repository
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm install my-db bitnami/postgresql    # Install PostgreSQL with one command!

# Customize with values
helm install my-db bitnami/postgresql \
  --set auth.postgresPassword=mypass \
  --set primary.persistence.size=10Gi

# Manage releases
helm list                                # List installed charts
helm upgrade my-db bitnami/postgresql    # Upgrade to new version
helm rollback my-db 1                    # Rollback to revision 1
helm uninstall my-db                     # Remove everything

Interview: 'Why use Helm?' Answer: It templatizes Kubernetes manifests, manages versions and rollbacks, handles complex dependency chains, and lets you install battle-tested community charts instead of reinventing the wheel.

quiz.question: What is Helm in the Kubernetes ecosystem?
options: A package manager for Kubernetes that simplifies deploying complex applications
quiz.explanation: Helm is the package manager for K8s. Charts are pre-configured packages of K8s YAML manifests. 'helm install my-db bitnami/postgresql' deploys an entire database setup with one command.

content.value: **Rolling Updates** let you deploy new versions with zero downtime. Kubernetes gradually replaces old Pods with new ones — like changing tires on a car while it's still driving (but safely).

content.title: Rolling Update Sequence
content.value:
sequenceDiagram participant D as Deployment participant Old as Old Pods (v1) participant New as New Pods (v2) D->>New: Create 1 new Pod (v2) New->>D: Health check passed ✅ D->>Old: Terminate 1 old Pod (v1) D->>New: Create 2nd new Pod (v2) New->>D: Health check passed ✅ D->>Old: Terminate 2nd old Pod (v1) D->>New: Create 3rd new Pod (v2) New->>D: Health check passed ✅ D->>Old: Terminate last old Pod (v1) Note over D,New: Rolling update complete!
Zero downtime achieved.

**Health Probes** tell Kubernetes how to check if your application is healthy:

- **Liveness Probe** — 'Is the app alive?' If it fails, K8s restarts the container.
- **Readiness Probe** — 'Is the app ready to receive traffic?' If it fails, K8s removes it from the Service load balancer.
- **Startup Probe** — 'Has the app finished starting up?' Gives slow-starting apps extra time.

content.title: Health Probes Configuration
content.value:
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:v2
      ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /health
          port: 3000
        initialDelaySeconds: 10
        periodSeconds: 15
        failureThreshold: 3
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /ready
          port: 3000
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 5
      startupProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /health
          port: 3000
        failureThreshold: 30
        periodSeconds: 10

content.title: Rolling Update Commands
content.value:
# Update image version (triggers rolling update)
kubectl set image deployment/web-app nginx=nginx:1.26

# Watch rollout progress
kubectl rollout status deployment/web-app

# Rollback if something goes wrong
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web-app

# View rollout history
kubectl rollout history deployment/web-app

Interview question: 'How do you achieve zero-downtime deployments in Kubernetes?' Answer: Use Rolling Updates (default strategy) with properly configured Readiness Probes. K8s only sends traffic to new pods after the readiness probe passes, ensuring users never hit an unready pod.

quiz.question: What happens if a Pod's liveness probe fails repeatedly?
options: An alert is sent to the admin
quiz.explanation: If the liveness probe fails more than the failureThreshold, Kubernetes kills the container and restarts it. This provides automatic recovery from application deadlocks or hangs.
